name: security-gym-v4
description: SCORING DEMO with fabricated metadata, not the authors' record. Ground-truth-labeled Linux server log and eBPF kernel-event streams for cybersecurity continual reinforcement learning research. The v4 dataset contains 11.2M base benign events (real Linux server traffic from four personal servers plus 24-hour eBPF kernel-event collections from three Debian 13 servers) plus 60,468 attack campaign events across six MITRE ATT&CK-aligned attack modules executed against a purpose-built lab VM. Composed into four pre-mixed experiment streams ranging from 4.9M to 257.7M events with Poisson-scheduled attack injection. Designed for use with the security-gym Gymnasium environment (`SecurityLogStream-Text-v0` and `SecurityLogStream-Hybrid-v0` observation modes).
citeAs: @dataset{lawson_security_gym_dataset_2026, author = {Lawson, Keith and Malik, Hafiz}, title = {Security-Gym Dataset: Labeled Linux Log and eBPF Streams for Continual Learning Research}, version = {4.1}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.21763493}, url = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21763493}, license = {Apache-2.0}}
rai:dataCollection: Benign traffic was collected from four personal Linux servers running standard services (SSH, nginx, syslog) operated by the dataset author. eBPF kernel events were collected over 24-hour windows on three Debian 13 servers (a hypervisor, a public web server, and a GPU lab server) via BCC tracepoints (sys_enter_execve, sched_process_exit, sys_enter_connect, sys_enter_accept4, sys_enter_openat, sys_enter_unlinkat). Attack traffic was generated by 10 scripted campaigns executed by a purpose-built campaign orchestrator against a deliberately vulnerable Debian 11 lab VM. No third-party infrastructure was probed. The University of Michigan-Dearborn IRB reviewed the collection protocol (HUM-DEMO-0001) and determined it exempt under 45 CFR 46.104(d)(4) as secondary research on information collected for non-research purposes; the exemption explicitly covers release for AI/ML training and benchmarking. The servers' published privacy notice informs visitors that access logs may be used for security research. All data came from systems the author operates; no third-party systems were accessed and nothing was obtained by deception or coercion.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw text log lines (auth.log, syslog, nginx access/error) and raw eBPF event dumps. Stored verbatim in the events.raw_line column.
rai:syntheticDataGeneration: All malicious events are synthetic, generated by a custom Python campaign orchestrator that executes 10 scripted MITRE ATT&CK-aligned attack campaigns (six modules: brute_force, web_attack, recon, malware, dos, lateral_movement) against an isolated UTM-virtualised Debian 11 lab VM. Benign events are real Linux server logs (auth.log, syslog, nginx access/error) and eBPF kernel events recorded from the dataset author's own servers, then PII-scrubbed and screened with MaliciousFilter to remove signature-matched attacks. Composed experiment streams further inject the synthetic attack events into the real benign baseline at MITRE ATT&CK-weighted Poisson-scheduled rates via StreamComposer. No third-party traffic, no production telemetry, no LLM-generated content.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Attack labeling uses CampaignLabeler with time-window + source-IP matching: an event is labeled malicious if its timestamp falls within an attack phase's window AND its src_ip matches an attacker IP for that phase. Events with no src_ip (e.g., syslog daemon messages) match on time window alone. eBPF kernel events use the same labeler. Benign events are filtered with MaliciousFilter using deterministic web/auth signature rules (path traversal, SQL injection, XSS, JNDI injection, RFI, scanner user-agents, failed-password sequences) before inclusion in the benign baseline. PII scrubbing applies case-insensitive hostname/domain/IP replacement to a single synthetic target identity (`isildur` / `192.168.2.201`).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom Python pipeline (campaign orchestrator + CampaignLabeler + MaliciousFilter)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All composed streams pass nine automated validation checks: (1) label consistency (is_malicious=1 implies non-NULL attack_type/stage/severity), (2) raw-line spot checks via regex per attack type, (3) campaign boundary containment, (4) campaign-type cross-validation, (5) target-array consistency for the SecurityGymStream adapter, (6) attack-type distribution against composition weights, (7) temporal order monotonicity, (8) no unlabeled events, (9) session coherence (all events in a session share the same is_malicious label). The checks are implemented in https://github.com/j-klawson/security-gym/blob/v0.4.2/scripts/validate_labels.py. Two security analysts independently relabelled 2,000 randomly sampled events (1,000 benign, 1,000 malicious): agreement with the automated labels was 99.65% (Cohen's kappa 0.97); all disagreements were time-window-only matches.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Compressed with Zstandard. Composed experiment streams are produced by StreamComposer with per-stream MITRE ATT&CK-aligned Poisson-scheduled attack injection and 24.2% eBPF downsampling. The streams are evaluated online in temporal order, so no train/validation/test split is defined; each stream's composition seed is recorded in its composition_meta table (99 for the 30-day stream). Nothing was withheld apart from the scrubbing described under personal information.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Versioned via Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18901541 always resolves to latest; v4.1 frozen at 10.5281/zenodo.21763493). HuggingFace mirror updated on each Zenodo version bump. Issues tracked at https://github.com/j-klawson/security-gym/issues. Data management plan: Keith Lawson is the data steward, with UM-Dearborn Library Research Data Services as successor steward. Zenodo retains every version for at least 20 years; the maintainers commit to updates for 5 years after v4.1 (through 2031). Deprecated versions stay downloadable with a deprecation notice naming the replacement. Changes in law or repository policy, and removal requests, are reviewed by the data access committee within 30 days and recorded in the release notes. Roadmap: https://github.com/j-klawson/security-gym/blob/main/ROADMAP.md
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Server hostnames, domains and addresses are mapped to one synthetic target identity (isildur / 192.168.2.201), and attack traffic uses lab-private 192.168.2.x addresses. Benign web-access and SSH log lines keep the remote client's source IP: in the 30-day stream 860,529 benign rows carry one of 11,413 distinct public IPv4 addresses (crawlers, scanners and other visitors), in both src_ip and raw_line. A privacy impact assessment by UM-Dearborn Information Security (March 2026) rated the retained public IPs low risk: they are not linked to names, accounts or content beyond the requested URL, and most belong to crawlers and scanners. Re-identification risk is reassessed annually and whenever a new linkage source (such as a public IP-to-identity dataset) appears; any address can be removed on request through the data access committee.
rai:dataBiases: Single-host scope (one target server). Benign baselines reflect the dataset author's personal infrastructure (academic / Linux developer profile), not enterprise fleet behavior. Benign load patterns may underrepresent enterprise SOC telemetry diversity. Class imbalance: 2.8% of events in the 30-day stream are malicious, so accuracy is dominated by the benign class; report per-class recall and PR-AUC. Events with no source IP are labelled by time window alone, which can mark concurrent benign daemon messages as malicious; an audit puts this at 0.3% of malicious labels. Attack timing follows a Poisson schedule, so models may learn the schedule rather than the attack content.
rai:dataLimitations: Six attack modules cover only a small subset of the MITRE ATT&CK technique space. Persistence, privilege escalation, and exfiltration modules are planned but not yet implemented. The benchmark does not test zero-day generalization (all attack modules are known TTPs) or multi-host lateral movement. The defense state (blocklist, throttle list, isolation mode) is simulated within the environment, not connected to a real firewall. eBPF events are downsampled to 24.2% during stream composition to simulate a single busy server, preserving event-type distributions but losing some inter-event temporal correlation.
rai:dataUseCases: Streaming continual reinforcement learning research; online representation learning from raw text and structured kernel-event streams; streaming deep-RL technique validation (LMS, ObGD, EMA normalization, sparse initialization); reward design in observation-suppressing environments; comparative evaluation of detection approaches (learned vs. rule-based) on non-stationary data.
rai:dataNotIntendedUseCases: Production SOC tooling. Models of enterprise infrastructure. Zero-day generalization evaluation. Substitutes for real-world deployment validation. Multi-host lateral-movement studies. The bundled attack modules target a purpose-built lab VM (`isildur`) and must not be directed at third-party infrastructure.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Research benchmark for continual learning on real cybersecurity telemetry. Releases otherwise unavailable PII-scrubbed Linux server traces with both traditional log channels and eBPF kernel events to enable academic reproduction of streaming-RL results in cybersecurity defense.

prov:wasDerivedFrom.name: mitre-attack-enterprise-matrix
prov:wasDerivedFrom.description: Source taxonomy of adversary tactics and techniques. Each Security-Gym attack campaign maps to one or more ATT&CK technique IDs (T1110 brute force, T1190 web exploitation, T1046 service discovery, T1059.004 unix shell, T1499 endpoint DoS, T1021 remote services). Used as the conceptual seed for the synthetic attack campaign design and for the per-stream attack-type distributions in StreamComposer. License compatibility: MITRE ATT&CK terms permit redistribution and derivative works with attribution; Security-Gym only inherits ATT&CK technique identifiers, not the underlying ATT&CK content.

prov:wasDerivedFrom.name: security-gym-campaigns
prov:wasDerivedFrom.alternateName: Security-Gym campaign configurations and orchestrator (synthetic-data seeds)
prov:wasDerivedFrom.description: Per-campaign YAML configurations specifying attack phases, timing profiles (constant, accelerating, burst), and target identities, plus the Python campaign orchestrator that consumes them. These two artifacts are the deterministic seeds for the synthetic attack events in this dataset: reproducible regeneration of any released stream requires only the configs, the orchestrator code, and a fixed RNG seed. No language models or other generative models were used in attack-event synthesis.

recordSet.name: events
recordSet.description: All streams share the same `events` table schema (single-table SQLite database). Each row is one telemetry event with ground-truth labels.

field.name: id
field.description: Auto-incrementing event identifier within the database.

field.name: timestamp
field.description: ISO 8601 UTC timestamp of the event.

field.name: raw_line
field.description: Original log line or eBPF event text as captured.

field.name: parsed
field.description: JSON-encoded parsed fields. Never NULL in the 30-day stream.

annotation.name: mean
annotation.description: Share of malicious events in exp_30d_heavy_v4.

field.name: attack_type
field.description: One of `brute_force` (T1110.001), `credential_stuffing` (T1110.004), `discovery` (T1046), `web_exploit` (T1190), or `execution` (T1059.004). NULL for benign events.

field.name: attack_stage
field.description: MITRE ATT&CK kill-chain stage label. NULL for benign events.

field.name: severity
field.description: Threat severity on a 1-5 scale (1-3 occur in the 30-day stream). NULL for benign events.

field.name: session_id
field.description: Session identifier for events that map to a session (e.g., SSH sessions).

field.name: src_ip
field.description: Source IP address (PII-scrubbed for benign events).

field.name: username
field.description: Username on authentication and session events.

examples.events/raw_line: May 20 19:08:27 clock-setup: rdate: adjust local clock by 75235016.224164 seconds
2026-03-20T16:16:03.752607Z execve pid=9833 ppid=1317 uid=0 comm=sshd parent_comm=sshd args=/usr/lib/openssh/sshd-session
Mar  1 18:03:50 isildur sshd[1902]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session closed for user researcher

rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Measured on the 30-day stream (21,511,208 rows): campaign_id, attack_type, attack_stage and severity are NULL on exactly the 20,901,688 benign rows and populated on all 609,520 malicious rows; is_malicious, timestamp, source, raw_line and parsed are never NULL. src_ip is NULL on 20,112,710 rows (93.5%), session_id on 20,476,710, username on 21,504,142 and service on 21,474,130, because most events (eBPF file/process records, syslog daemon messages) have no client address, session or user. NULL is the only missing-value marker; no empty strings are used.

odrl:permission.name: Research, teaching and benchmarking of detection and continual-learning methods, including AI/ML training.

odrl:prohibition.name: Re-identifying, contacting or profiling the holders of public IP addresses in the logs.
Using the data to plan or run attacks on the logged hosts or any third party.
Redistributing subsets that isolate individual visitors' activity.
